q: Which function of money does the lecturer treat as central, logically prior to the others?
explain: Debts and prices must be expressed in a unit of account before anything can discharge them (Keynes, Treatise).

q: The Latin word 'pecunia' (money) comes from the word for…
explain: In pastoral societies debts and credits were recorded and accepted in animals: money is tied to debt and credit from the start.

q: In which year did the dollar–gold link end?
explain: Because of US balance-of-payments problems; after that money has no reference to any commodity.

q: What does Peel's Bank Act (1844) illustrate, according to the lecturer?
options: Tying note issue strictly to gold reserves did not work: people invent substitutes
That the gold standard guarantees stable prices
That central banks should finance the Treasury
That bank money is outside money
explain: Strict quantity rules lose control of interest rates and trigger financial innovation ('if you need money, you invent something').

q: With no commodity anchor, what guarantees money's value?
options: The state, which defines the unit of account in which debts and taxes are discharged
Gold reserves at the central bank
explain: Whether expressed in a commodity or fiat is secondary: the state's definition of the unit of account is the essential element.

q: In Keynes's Treatise, 'money proper' is…
options: The thing that answers to the description given by the money of account
The description or title (e.g. 'the pound sterling')
explain: Money of account = description/title; money proper = the thing that answers to it. The state decides which thing does.

q: Bank money is fiduciary: it circulates only as long as people trust that the private debt will be honoured.
explain: This distinguishes it from legal tender, which only the state can issue.

q: Which of these is inside money?
explain: A deposit is an asset for one private agent and a liability for another (the bank), so private net wealth is unchanged.

q: Outside money (state money) is…
options: A liability of the state but a net asset for the private sector
A liability of banks and an asset of firms
Created entirely within the private sector
explain: With it you can discharge debts to other people and to the state itself.

q: Creating inside money changes the net wealth of the private sector as a whole.
explain: Assets and liabilities are just reshuffled between private units. Keep apart the individual level and the system level.

q: Match each author to their position on the quantity theory and money.
pairs: Key representative of the quantity theory (marginalist)
Against it: money endogenous, interest rate set by real factors
Interest rate is monetary, money treated as exogenous
explain: Both approaches contain authors on each side of the quantity theory.

q: For Wicksell, the (natural) rate of interest is determined by…
explain: Money is endogenous in Wicksell, but the rate of interest is a real phenomenon.

q: Post-Keynesian and New Keynesian mean the same thing.
explain: Post-Keynesians are the economists closest to Keynes (the Cambridge Circus: Kaldor, Joan Robinson…).

q: Post-Keynesians (Kaldor, Lavoie…) hold that money is…
explain: Like Wicksell, and unlike Keynes in the General Theory, who treats money as exogenous.

q: At the most abstract level (value and distribution), the main divide in economic theory is between…
explain: Even economists within the same approach can disagree on money.

q: Match each emphasis to its consequence.
pairs: Price of money = the interest rate (opportunity cost)
Spectrum of liquidity; no sharp line for 'money'
explain: Which function you stress determines what you call money and what its price is.

q: Liquidity of an asset is…
options: How readily it can be used for payments or converted into other assets, and at what cost
Whether the central bank issued it
explain: A short-term bond is more liquid than a long-term bond, and both more than a building.

q: What happened when central banks tried to control M1 in the early 1980s?
explain: Controlling a quantity triggers substitution and financial innovation (compare Peel's Act).

q: Controlling the quantity of money by strict legal rules tends to…
options: Lose control of interest rates and trigger financial innovation
Remove the need for a unit of account
explain: The lecturer's reading of history: no strict commodity link is needed.

q: Why does the lecturer call central bank money a 'very peculiar' debt?
options: The state gave the central bank the power to issue legal tender, so it cannot fail like a private bank
It does not appear on any balance sheet
explain: Notes still appear as a liability, a legacy of when gold was the asset.

q: Keynes's term for central bank notes that first circulated alongside commodity money, with some link to reserves:
explain: Commodity and representative money are the two forms of state money in Keynes.

q: Which is NOT one of the three functions of money?
explain: The three functions are interlinked, but different approaches emphasise different ones.

q: In the lecturer's reconstruction, bank money originates from…
explain: As debt relations develop, acknowledgments of debt start to substitute for money.

q: Adam Smith's problem that money solves is…
options: The lack of a unit of account
explain: In Smith/Menger, money emerges spontaneously to reduce transaction costs; no unit of account and no state.

q: In the Smith–Menger account of the origin of money, the state and the unit of account play a central role.
explain: That is the credit/chartalist view (Keynes, Knapp, post-Keynesians).

q: The earliest forms of writing emerged to record…
options: Debts and credits (e.g. taxes due to the temple)
explain: Money predates writing; writing was developed to record debt.

q: According to Polanyi, debts originally arose from…
options: Social events such as marriage, killing, coming of age
explain: Economic transactions came later; early societies had gifts and debts.

q: Which German word is the standard example of the link between debt and guilt?
explain: In some languages the word for debt is etymologically linked to sin or guilt.

q: Standardised coinage was introduced in Egypt only under…
explain: Unit of account ≠ coins: the sovereign defines the unit without minting.

q: In China silver was first used as money in the form of…
explain: Silver coinage came later.

q: In a medieval tally stick, the creditor kept the longer piece, called the…
explain: 'Capital stock' and 'corporate stock' remind us of this. Tallies were transferable debt.

q: The English Exchequer used tally sticks to record loans and taxes until…
explain: Tallies circulated alongside coins.

q: The first coins were made of electrum. What does this suggest?
options: High purchasing power: payment tokens or evidence of debt, not everyday trade
They were for everyday market purchases
They were issued by private banks
explain: History highlights money's role as evidence of debt.

q: Knapp's 'The State Theory of Money' (1905) sees money as…
options: Evidence of debt owed to the state, including taxes
explain: That explains why the state defines the unit of account.

q: In Keynes's chartalism, 'writing the dictionary' means…
options: Specifying how much of a thing makes one unit of money
explain: 'Enforcing the dictionary' = enforcing that, say, gold is money. Together with minting, it completes state money.

q: Match each economist to their view on the state's role in money.
pairs: No state needed; private sector issues, no central bank
Money too important to leave to the private sector
State must define money and regulate its quantity
explain: Keynes and Friedman agree on this despite being theoretically far apart.

q: Seigniorage is…
options: The profit from reducing metal content while keeping the coin's nominal value (earned by the state)
explain: Today only the state or central bank can issue the monetary base.

q: Why did the state take direct control of minting?
options: Private minters tended to debase the coinage
explain: Sequence: private minters paying a fee → debasement → state control → paper money → fiat.

q: The lecturer considers Bitcoin to be money.
explain: A speculative instrument. Many stablecoins are too: the issued amount should relate to the monetary base or backing assets, which often isn't so.

q: Which is a reason the lecturer gives for the digital euro?
options: To cut the profits of private payment platforms and give the ECB some control
To replace the unit of account
explain: The holding limit exists so as not to crowd out the banking system, which finances investment and consumption.

q: The digital euro holding limit under discussion is about…
explain: The lecturer said around €3,000, 'still under discussion'. Purpose: not to drain bank deposits.

q: Weimar Germany and Argentina show that…
options: Money works as a medium of exchange only if the monetary standard is reasonably stable
Barter is more efficient than money
explain: With continuous strong losses of value people go back to barter or hold dollars.

q: With n goods, a numéraire reduces the relative prices you need to know from n(n−1)/2 to…
explain: All prices are expressed in the numéraire.

q: Inflation favours debtors and deflation favours creditors.
explain: That's why the choice of numéraire is not neutral.

q: Cheaper production of the numéraire (e.g. Potosí silver in the 16th century) makes…
options: Relative prices change but not the price level
explain: The price level depends on the conditions of production of the numéraire relative to those of all other goods.

q: The interwar debate on the numéraire for international exchange rates proposed…
explain: But which goods enter the bundle changes relative prices between countries: real effects.

q: If Italy left the euro for a new lira expected to depreciate, who would lose?
explain: Changing the unit of account redistributes.

q: Why hold wealth in money even though it pays no (or less) interest?
options: It has the greatest liquidity and certainty of its nominal value
It keeps real value under inflation
It is risk-free in real terms
explain: Not certainty of real value: inflation erodes it, as for other assets.

q: Which great Mediterranean traders began minting coins relatively late?
explain: They didn't need coins, or even money, for their trade.

q: Money predates writing.
explain: Writing emerged to record debts and credits (e.g. Egyptian temple taxes).

q: Which marginalist economist, with Adam Smith, locates money's origin in the medium-of-exchange function?
explain: Different approaches, same view on origin.

q: In Argentina's high inflation (~120%), the lecturer says the wealthy hold their wealth in…
explain: Others spend wages on goods as soon as they receive them.

q: Match the monetary aggregate to its content.
pairs: M1 + deposits with agreed maturity up to 2 years
M2 + repos, money market fund shares, short-term debt securities
explain: Each aggregate adds assets with lower liquidity.

q: A HIGH cross-elasticity of deposits with respect to the short-term interest rate implies…
options: It's hard to draw the line: a spectrum of liquidity
explain: Low elasticity → treat base money + deposits as 'money'.

q: Why did the Bank of England need M4 and M5?
options: After targeting M1/M2 (monetarism), other aggregates grew through financial innovation
explain: Controlling base money and deposits triggered innovation and growth of other financial assets.

q: Why does the ECB not include short-term government bonds in M3, unlike the old Bank of Italy?
options: Public bonds concern the public sector and say nothing about private-sector liquidity
explain: Italian households held BOTs as close substitutes for deposits (high cross-elasticity).

q: Which repos are excluded from M3?
options: Repos between a money market fund and a bank
explain: Within the banking sector they cancel out when you consolidate its balance sheet.

q: Why are repos between a non-bank (e.g. money market fund) and a bank counted in M3?
options: The fund's deposits fall (M2 falls) but total money hasn't changed: liquidity took another form
explain: Counting them in M3 captures the shift.

q: Reusing the same collateral for several operations is called…
explain: It raises system liquidity speculatively, adding risk, so central banks regulate it.

q: A haircut means that against a bond worth 100 the lender lends, say…
explain: The 20 margin protects against risk.

q: Why does the central bank's list of eligible collateral and haircuts matter?
options: It signals monetary policy: e.g. removing Greek bonds starves Greek banks of central bank funding
It determines the unit of account
explain: Collateral policy is a policy signal.

q: Neither Friedman nor Keynes ever precisely defined money.
explain: It becomes important for policy: 'if you say you must control money, which aggregate?'

q: A 'run towards liquidity' typically happens…
explain: Everyone sells less liquid assets to buy more liquid ones; money demand becomes very strong.

q: The monetarist idea of money is something specific that yields…
options: Services (indirect utility) because it lets you buy goods
explain: Lecturer's counterpoint: short-term bonds can be accepted in payment too; what matters is liquidity.

q: Why do central banks track several aggregates?
options: It is hard to say what money is, and to control it
explain: Strong substitutability between base money/deposits and short-term assets.

q: The first central banks (17th century) were…
options: The Riksbank (Sweden) and the Bank of England
The Bank of France and Reichsbank
The Fed and Bank of Japan
explain: They arose as financial markets needed regulating.

q: Which 'forgotten' central bank function does the lecturer mention?
options: Financing investment projects (e.g. Bank of France and infrastructure)
explain: Other historical functions: financing the state, regulating money and credit, lender of last resort, managing the exchange rate.

q: A currency appreciation tends to…
explain: The exchange rate affects capital flows, net exports and the price level.

q: Which central banks also aim to keep the economy near full employment?
options: The Fed and the Bank of Japan
explain: Price stability as the main goal is a modern view, not always historical.

q: Central bank goals (price stability, employment) can conflict.
explain: Raising the rate to bring inflation down hurts output and employment.

q: Harrod's [?] view of the 'optimal' policy:
options: Set the interest rate as low as possible
Target inflation relative to the natural rate
explain: Minimises debt-servicing cost and leaves room for expansionary fiscal policy. Name uncertain: check slides.

q: Today's dominant view of optimal monetary policy:
options: Target an inflation rate, setting the policy rate relative to the natural rate (sometimes by rules)
explain: A low rate is not necessarily best; price stability may require a higher one.

q: The monetary base is…
explain: CU = banknotes and coins in circulation (including cash held by banks); RE = banks' deposits at the central bank.

q: RE (reserves) in the monetary base are the public's deposits at commercial banks.
explain: They are banks' deposits at the central bank.

q: Who demands base money?
options: The public (cash) and banks (compulsory and discretionary reserves)
explain: Banks hold discretionary reserves against risk or liquidity needs.

q: Which is the MAIN channel of base-money creation?
explain: Banks structurally need base money for reserve requirements; the central bank exploits that to steer aggregates and rates.

q: Article 123 TFEU prohibits…
options: Overdrafts/credit to governments and direct (primary market) purchase of their debt
explain: The Treasury channel is closed in the euro area.

q: The Italian 'divorce' between the Bank of Italy and the Treasury was done by…
options: A letter from Governor Ciampi to the Treasury Minister (Andreatta)
explain: Early 1980s; not a decision of Parliament.

q: Ciampi's stated aim with the divorce:
options: A change of monetary regime to bring inflation down
explain: 'Monetary dominance' over fiscal policy: monetary policy must not finance fiscal policy directly.

q: The euro is described as…
options: A unit of account before having a state
A state without a unit of account
explain: Perhaps the first case in history; this caused problems.

q: Draghi's 'whatever it takes' was in…
explain: With 3% in Germany and 15% in Italy 'no monetary union can survive'. Words alone narrowed spreads.

q: The 'capital key' rule says ECB holdings of each country's public debt should be proportional to…
options: That country's national central bank's share of ECB capital
explain: It was respected at least on average, which helped the European Court rule QE legitimate.

q: A balance-of-payments surplus (foreign channel) leads to…
explain: Foreigners exchange dollars for euros: reserves up, euros in circulation up. Deficit → destroyed.

q: ECB reserve requirements are around…
options: 1%, met on average over a maintenance period
explain: Banks can use reserves day to day; the requirement applies to the most liquid deposits.

q: The MAIN reason to keep the reserve ratio low:
options: The interbank market becomes a sensitive indicator of system liquidity
explain: Other reasons: lower opportunity cost for banks, and flexibility.

q: If banks can count on the central bank for liquidity, they don't need large reserves; the question is the price, not availability.
explain: The marginal lending facility is the old discount window.

q: A central bank can let a very big financial institution fail without systemic risk.
explain: Banks are interconnected: one failure can bring down others. Smaller banks can fail; deposits are insured up to a limit.

q: QE purchases of government bonds by the ECB were made in the…
explain: The justification was the ECB mandate to ensure the survival and stability of the euro.

q: On financing governments, the Fed…
options: Doesn't finance individual states but supports federal bonds indirectly
Is forbidden to buy any bonds
explain: It buys in the secondary market and gives banks liquidity to buy federal bonds.

q: During COVID, the Fed and the Bank of England…
explain: The Bank of Japan doesn't follow the 'closed channel' rule either.

q: The old debate 'does the central bank set the money supply or the interest rate?' has a shared answer today:
explain: This comes back with the endogeneity of money.

q: Match each instrument to its description.
pairs: Buying/selling securities with no agreement to reverse: structural
Standing facility: the old discount window, rate above MRO
Standing facility: overnight deposits at a very low rate
explain: All operations are against collateral.

q: Open market operations are initiated by…, standing facilities by…
options: The central bank / the counterparty bank
The counterparty bank / the central bank
explain: Standing facilities are at the counterparty's initiative.

q: Bagehot (Lombard Street, 1873): lend to a bank in trouble…
explain: A bank needing such liquidity probably took on high risk, but you still help it to protect the whole system.

q: Why does the lecturer call negative rates on excess reserves 'not a brilliant idea'?
options: Reserves piled up not because banks misbehaved but because there was little loan demand with acceptable risk
explain: Reserves stay at the central bank or are used to buy government bonds.

q: In the corridor, the ceiling is the … rate and the floor is the … rate.
explain: The MRO rate sits in the middle; the interbank overnight rate oscillates around it.

q: The corridor as a signal: all three rates going UP means…
explain: A narrow corridor means the central bank tolerates less fluctuation in the interbank rate.

q: What defines a floor system?
options: The policy (MRO) rate coincides with the deposit rate
The policy rate equals the ceiling
explain: Banks are indifferent between lending reserves and holding them at the central bank.

q: The floor system was adopted by England from…, the US from…, the ECB from…
explain: The ECB moved more slowly (Trichet even raised rates in 2011); the Fed was the most innovative.

q: The advantage of a floor system for QE:
options: The central bank can inject large liquidity without having to withdraw it or change the policy rate
explain: Excess reserves are simply held at the central bank.

q: Strategy at the zero lower bound:
options: Set the nominal rate at zero and raise inflation expectations, so the real rate falls below a negative natural rate
explain: The worry in those years was deflation, not inflation.

q: In a fixed-rate tender, allotment is…, and the problem is…
explain: A bank can borrow at, say, 3% and lend at 4% in the interbank market, so it asks for more than it needs.

q: In a variable-rate tender…
options: Bids are filled from the highest rate down, above a minimum bid rate; the marginal rate is allotted pro rata
All banks pay the same rate
Rates are set by the Treasury
explain: This discourages overbidding: cheap liquidity is no longer guaranteed.

q: The 'discount window stigma' is that…
options: Banks in stress avoid it for fear of damaging their reputation
explain: But if it really needs liquidity, a bank goes anyway: 'sometimes you prefer a bad reputation to failing'.

q: Fed practice at the discount window:
options: First time above the usual rate, second time higher, eventually 'stop'
Always lends at the same rate
explain: The central bank usually provides liquidity to avoid failures, especially of big banks.

q: Real short-term rates in the 1970s were…
explain: Inflation was very high even though nominal rates weren't zero. Late 1970s: very restrictive monetary and fiscal policy.

q: In the 1980s the central banks ran a floor system.
explain: The floor system came with QE after 2007–08.

q: On the 'conflict' view of inflation, the early-1980s restrictive policy worked by…
options: Raising unemployment and weakening workers' bargaining power
explain: Together with labour market reforms in Italy, the US and the UK (Thatcher).

q: Compared with the 1970s, in the recent imported-inflation episode in Italy…
options: The cost fell on wages and real wages fell
Real wages grew fastest in history
explain: 1970s: highest real wage growth despite oil and lira depreciation (strong bargaining power).

q: The suggested short essay on inflation compares the 1970s and today through…
explain: Who bears the burden of a worsening of the terms of trade?

q: 'Short-term' vs 'short run': which is correct?
options: Short-term = maturity of an asset; short run = period with given productive capacity
explain: A referee once caught the lecturer writing 'short-run interest rate' for 'short-term'.

q: Transmission chain of policy:
options: Central bank → overnight interbank → savings deposits → short-term bonds → long-term bonds
Long bonds → short bonds → interbank → central bank
explain: Linked by no-arbitrage conditions.

q: In crises, short and long rates…
options: Can diverge, so the central bank intervenes in specific market segments
explain: The central bank's goal is a certain structure of rates (2% short with 20% long would conflict with its goals).

q: Approximately, nominal rate i =
explain: (1+i) = (1+r)(1+π^e); r·π^e is negligible. E.g. nominal 5%, expected inflation 2% → real ≈ 3%.

q: A 'Fisher effect' can be spoken of only if…
options: The real rate is determined by real factors (e.g. productivity)
explain: Causality then runs from real rate and inflation to the nominal rate (marginalist models).

q: If the interest rate is a monetary phenomenon and the central bank keeps the nominal rate fixed, a rise in inflation…
explain: Expected inflation can still matter if the central bank reacts, but as a policy choice, not a mechanical adjustment.

q: The three theories of the term structure are…
explain: The expectations theory is the basis for the other two.

q: The 'structural' approach to the yield curve (rates from supply and demand for each asset) is associated with…
explain: Usually a reduced form (long rate as function of the short rate) is used instead.

q: The expectations theory says the expected return of the strategies must be the same…
options: Only in equilibrium with forward markets
explain: Long horizon: buy long or roll over short. Short horizon: buy short or buy long and sell before maturity.

q: If expected short rates are constant (no premium), the yield curve is…
explain: Expected to rise → R > r (upward); expected to fall → R < r (downward).

q: What can pure expectations theory NOT explain?
options: Why the yield curve is usually upward-sloping
Why the curve can be flat
Why long rates depend on short rates
explain: It would need short rates to be expected to rise most of the time.

q: Match the author to their contribution to the term structure.
pairs: Error-learning and a risk element rising with maturity
explain: The risk element and the liquidity premium usually put together explain the upward slope.

q: In Meiselman's model the risk element z is…
explain: Long-term asset prices are more variable → bigger capital-loss risk. Even with constant expected short rates, R > r.

q: Meiselman's 'error-learning' mechanism has expectations revised after…
options: A forecast error on the current rate, applied to all future expected rates
A change in the exchange rate
explain: The lecturer finds it 'very strange', but it was the first explicit mechanism. Check the formula against the slides.

q: In preferred habitat, if the majority of investors is risk-averse, the curve is…
explain: Moving out of your habitat requires a premium. With risk-lovers you could get the opposite.

q: Hicks's liquidity premium: borrowers prefer to borrow…, lenders prefer to lend…
explain: So lenders need a premium to lend long; otherwise they'd hold money or very short assets.

q: The US 10-year minus 3-month Treasury spread was negative (an inverted curve) around…
explain: Some economists read an inverted curve as the market expecting a crisis, with short rates expected to be cut.

q: For Keynes, the central bank can influence long rates by…
options: Shaping expectations of future short rates (needing consistent policy)
explain: The rate is highly conventional: any level accepted with conviction as durable will be durable.

q: For the marginalist (Wicksellian) view, the central bank can influence long rates…
options: Only temporarily: the market rate adjusts to the natural rate (productivity and thrift)
explain: Productivity is behind the demand for capital, thrift behind its supply.

q: Keynes's idea that the interest rate is conventional comes from which text?
explain: Quote reconstructed from the notes; check wording against the slides.

q: In some post-Keynesian strands, monetary authorities can set the real interest rate and thereby affect…
explain: Both Keynes and post-Keynesians share the idea; the adjustment mechanism differs (not via investment and output in the post-Keynesian case).

q: Keynes (General Theory) suggested that the central bank might…
options: Buy and sell gilt-edged bonds of all maturities at stated prices
explain: So 'unconventional' policy is not new. Wording reconstructed: check slides.

q: The two routes by which the central bank steers the long rate:
options: Expectations (consistent announcements) and risk (purchases in specific markets)
explain: Matching the two components: average expected short rates, and the risk element.

q: When is route 2 (purchases acting on the risk element) needed?
options: When the central bank cuts the short rate and promises an accommodative policy but the long rate rises anyway
explain: Expectations alone have failed: typically in a crisis.

q: A long-term bond is e.g. a…, short-term assets are e.g. …
explain: Short-term: 3 months to a year, traditionally held by Italian households.

q: Meiselman's formulation for the real yield curve: R ≈ avg real expected short rates + avg expected inflation + …
explain: Even without believing in the Fisher effect, inflation can pass into nominal rates.

q: Under perfect certainty, the compounded long-rate return over n periods equals…
explain: No-arbitrage: borrow short and invest long (or vice versa) until equality holds.

q: Stock vs flow:
options: A flow occurs over a period; a stock is measured at a point in time
A stock occurs over a period; a flow at a point in time
Both are measured at a point in time
explain: Investment (flow) changes the capital stock.

q: Final stock =
explain: Revaluations (price changes) are ignored in the simple model.

q: The sectoral balances identity is a causal relationship.
explain: Ex post identity: whether G crowds out I or C depends on whether output can change.

q: Private + government + rest-of-world financial balances =
explain: One sector's net lending is another's net borrowing.

q: If output can rise, a rise in G…
options: Raises Y and hence S, with no necessary crowding out
explain: If output is given at potential, G ↑ must reduce C or I.

q: Stock-flow consistent (SFC) models are mainly associated with…
explain: All stocks and flows are made explicit; a full model = accounting framework + behavioural equations.

q: In the simple closed-economy model, households hold deposits and bills only, no cash. So the monetary base is…
explain: Four sectors: households, firms, banks, consolidated public sector.

q: Retained (non-distributed) profits are…
options: Firm saving, which can finance investment without bank loans
explain: Excluded from the simple model by assuming all profits are distributed.

q: In the balance sheet matrix, only … has no counterpart liability.
explain: Financial rows sum to zero; K is 'by definition the wealth of a nation'.

q: Who denies that public debt is part of private wealth?
explain: Households anticipate future taxes to service the debt.

q: Sign convention in the transactions-flow matrix:
options: Receipts and sources of funds +; expenditures and acquisitions of financial assets −
explain: Convention as described in class; matrices were reconstructed. Check the slides.

q: A subscript −1 in the transactions matrix (e.g. r·B₋₁) refers to…
options: The stock at the end of the previous period
explain: Interest this period is paid on the stock held at the start.

q: Stocks feed back on flows because…
options: Debts generate interest flows and wealth affects consumption and portfolio decisions
explain: Tobin: agents want certain proportions of assets in total wealth.

q: Net private saving must materialise as…
options: Real capital (ΔK) or claims on the public sector (ΔB, ΔH)
explain: Private claims net out within the private sector.

q: A sector's financial balance over a period is positive when it is a net…
explain: Net borrowing (−) increases liabilities relative to assets.

q: The first clear statement of the quantity theory was by…
options: Jean Bodin (16th century), after the Potosí silver
explain: It is usually ascribed to Hume.

q: MV = PT is an accounting identity that all economists accept.
explain: It becomes a theory only with assumptions on which variables are given and the direction of causality.

q: Which is NOT an assumption of the quantity theory?
explain: V and T independent; in Keynes's General Theory a change in income can change V.

q: In the quantity theory causality runs from… to …; with endogenous money it reverses.
explain: A rise in the general price level requires a change in M; otherwise only relative prices change.

q: Why is V taken as given?
options: Institutional factors (payment arrangements, vertical integration, synchronisation of receipts and payments)
explain: The more vertically integrated production, the lower V.

q: Why is output (T or Y) taken as given?
pairs: Say's law: saving becomes investment, capacity used at the desired degree (not full employment)
Full employment through wage flexibility and factor substitution
explain: Compare Stirati 10_07.

q: In the Cambridge version M_d = kPY, k equals…
explain: The public holds balances in proportion to income, to plan transactions (transactions demand, also in Keynes).

q: The quantity theory implies money is…
options: Neutral: a veil that doesn't affect real variables
explain: Classical dichotomy: real sector determines quantities and relative prices; monetary sector the general price level.

q: Sidrauski's model features…
options: Money in the utility function, no dichotomy, yet super-neutrality
Money as a veil with dichotomy
explain: Super-neutrality: even the growth rate of money doesn't affect real steady-state variables. Equilibrium conditions: not covered yet.

q: Friedman's 1956 restatement is titled…
options: The Quantity Theory of Money: A Restatement
A Monetary History of the US
explain: It treats money as an asset demanded for its services.

q: Friedman's main thesis on money demand:
options: A stable function of real (permanent) income, with the interest rate not the main determinant
Very sensitive to the interest rate

q: Which is NOT in Friedman's list of determinants of money demand?
options: Share of non-human capital in total wealth
explain: Human capital is measured by capitalising labour income.

q: Permanent income comes from Friedman's analysis of … and implies … multiplier than Keynes supposed.
explain: Consumption depends on average income; a transitory rise in income need not raise consumption.

q: Friedman makes wealth operational by replacing it with…
options: Permanent income, whose present value is wealth
explain: Permanent income = average income, excluding transitory components.
